Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s rising political violence and growing threats to institutional independence could weaken investor confidence, trigger capital flight, and increase business operating costs ahead of the 2027 general elections, the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE) has warned. The organisation said escalating political tensions, intimidation, and inflammatory rhetoric posed significant economic risks, particularly as the country continues to navigate economic reforms and efforts to attract domestic and foreign investment. In a policy brief signed by Muda Yusuf, chief executive officer of CPPE, the organisation warned that political instability could discourage fresh investments, delay business expansion, and increase the risk premiums demanded by investors. “Political violence is not merely a threat to democratic governance; it constitutes a significant economic risk with far-reaching consequences,” the brief stated. According to the CPPE, prolonged political instability could weaken investor sentiment, trigger portfolio outflows and intensify foreign exchange volatility, adding pressure to an already vulnerable investment environment. It also warned that political clashes, insecurity, and violent protests could disrupt commercial activities, supply chains, logistics and market access, while forcing businesses to spend more on security, insurance, transportation, and contingency arrangements. The organisation said small businesses, informal enterprises, and investors with significant fixed assets were particularly exposed because their operations and investments could not easily be relocated. Beyond the direct economic consequences of violence, the CPPE identified the neutrality of state institutions as critical to maintaining investor confidence during the electoral cycle. It urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), security agencies and the judiciary to operate independently and professionally, warning against political interference, selective enforcement and the use of regulatory institutions to intimidate opponents. Read also: Nigeria risks fossil-fuel trap as global AI industry turns to greener data centres “The politicisation of these institutions creates risks that extend well beyond the electoral process,” the brief stated. It added that institutional interference weakens the rule of law, undermines regulatory predictability, and increases perceptions of arbitrary government action, eroding confidence in the protection of investments and contractual rights. The CPPE also called on political parties and their leaders to publicly reject violence, restrain their supporters and cooperate with lawful investigations and prosecution of offenders. It urged political leaders to avoid inflammatory statements and ensure that security arrangements protect commercial centres, industrial facilities, transport corridors, markets and critical infrastructure throughout the electoral period. The organisation further warned against disruptions to economic governance, regulatory institutions and existing contractual and investment commitments arising from political competition. “The conduct of political actors and the integrity of state institutions during the 2027 electoral cycle will be important determinants of Nigeria’s political risk profile and investment outlook,” it said. The CPPE maintained that peaceful political competition, credible institutions, and respect for the rule of law would help sustain investor confidence, protect business continuity and preserve economic stability. It warned that allowing electoral ambition to override national economic interests could undermine the gains of ongoing reforms and weaken Nigeria’s attractiveness to investors.
